title: Single Cell RNA-seq Workshop
text:
Welcome to the Center for Biomedical Data Science Single Cell RNA-seq Workshop — a hands-on, three-day workshop that takes you end-to-end through a modern single-cell RNA-seq analysis: from count matrices through quality control, clustering, cell-type annotation, multi-sample integration, and differential expression. By the end you’ll be able to produce and interpret a figure like the clustered UMAP above. The workshop is sponsored by the Center for Biomedical Data Science (CBDS) at the University of Oregon.
This site hosts everything the workshop runs on — lecture slides, hands-on tutorials, datasets, and reference material — and it stays online as a free, living resource for your continued learning long after the workshop ends.
Use the navigation bar above to reach the schedule, software setup, all workshop materials, and additional resources.



 Back to top

title: Software Setup
text: Get your laptop ready before Day 1. Plan 30–60 minutes the day before — not the morning of. The optional Day 0 session is the place to bring any install problems you can’t solve yourself.

title: Software Setup
text:
1. Required tools

R ≥ 4.4 — download
RStudio Desktop (current release) — download
VS Code (current release) — download

title: Software Setup
text:
2. Install command-line tools
Several R / Bioconductor packages compile from source the first time you install them, which needs a working command-line compiler toolchain; the command-line portions of the workshop also assume a POSIX shell. Set this up once, for your operating system. The command line itself — navigating, pipes, grep — is covered in Appendix B and Appendix F, and the optional Day 0 walks through it; if a package later fails to build, the FAQ lists the usual fixes.
macOS — open the built-in Terminal (Applications → Utilities), or install iTerm2 for a nicer one, then install Apple’s Xcode command-line tools:
xcode-select --install
This provides clang, git, make, and the headers R needs to build packages. Some packages also need a Fortran compiler — if you later hit gfortran not found, install gfortran for macOS. Re-launch RStudio after it finishes.
Windows — install Rtools, the toolchain that lets Windows build R packages from source, from https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/ (pick the version matching your R — e.g. Rtools44 for R 4.4). For the shell/command-line portions of the workshop, also install WSL2 + Ubuntu, which gives you a real POSIX shell:

Run PowerShell as Administrator.
wsl --install -d ubuntu and press Enter. Restart when prompted.
Launch Ubuntu from the Start menu and set a username and password.
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

Full Microsoft guide: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install. If you run R inside WSL rather than native Windows, see the FAQ note on where to keep your project files.
Linux — use your built-in terminal and install the build toolchain from your package manager. On Ubuntu/Debian:
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y build-essential gfortran
build-essential provides gcc, g++, and make; gfortran covers packages with Fortran code. On Fedora/RHEL, use sudo dnf groupinstall "Development Tools" plus gcc-gfortran.

title: Software Setup
text:
3. Install the R packages
The R / Bioconductor packages the workshop uses — along with a short primer on how packages, updates, LaTeX, and Quarto work — are covered in Tutorial 00 — Get Up and Running with R, RStudio & Quarto. We do it together at the very start of Day 1, but because the first install can take 20–60 minutes, we recommend opening Tutorial 00 and running its install block before you arrive.

title: Software Setup
text:
Something didn’t work?
The FAQ documents the issues that come up most often: Mac compiler errors, BiocManager mirror selection, RStudio caching old library paths, etc.

title: scNotebooks ↔︎ Workshop Crosswalk
text:
scNotebooks is an open, multilingual (English / Spanish / Portuguese) Jupyter-notebook curriculum for single-cell and spatial genomics, developed by the Integrative Bioinformatics group in collaboration with the Human Cell Atlas, LatinCells, and Wellcome Connecting Sciences. It runs as 13 modules, each a self-contained .ipynb you can open in Google Colab or run locally with their Docker image.
This page maps each of their modules to the corresponding tutorial(s) and lecture(s) in our workshop, so you can use scNotebooks as a parallel-language companion or as a feeder for topics we don’t yet cover. Both curricula use Seurat in R as the main scRNA-seq toolkit, and both use the same canonical ifnb dataset for integration teaching.

title: scNotebooks ↔︎ Workshop Crosswalk
text:
Direct correspondences
The first five scNotebooks modules cover the same workflow as our Tutorials 01–08. Module 10 (Spatial) maps to our Tutorial 11. Module 11 (scATAC) is the ArchR alternative to our Signac-based Tutorial 09.



scNotebooks module
Workshop equivalent
Notes




Module 01 — Notebooks & databases (html)
Appendix I — Gene-Expression Databases & File Formats
We don’t reproduce the Jupyter / Colab introduction (Quarto plays that role for our workshop), but we adapted their database tour into a written field guide covering the big-six repositories (GEO, SRA, SCEA, HCA, CELLxGENE, PanglaoDB / CellTypist), expanded with a detailed file-format reference (FASTQ, mtx, h5, fragments.tsv.gz, AnnData, .rds), and a hands-on exploration exercise.


Module 02 — Intro to R + ggplot2 (html)
Appendix A — R Programming
Their walkthrough is in Colab; ours is a Quarto reference chapter you read alongside RStudio. The R-side topics from Module 02 — lists / matrices / factors as data structures, named vs positional arguments, dplyr verbs, ggplot2 grammar of graphics — are all covered in Appendix A’s later sections.


Module 03 — Cell Ranger / raw-seq processing (html)
Talapas Advanced — Raw RNA Cell Ranger + Talapas Advanced — Raw ATAC
We adapted this for SLURM on Talapas. The laptop sequence still starts at the filtered Cell Ranger output (so beginners aren’t blocked); the Talapas Advanced tutorials walk cellranger count and cellranger-atac count as batch jobs once you have your own raw FASTQs.


Module 04 — QC, clustering, annotation, functional analysis (html)
Tutorials 01 + 02 + 03 + 07 functional analysis + 08 differential abundance + 04 reference annotation
scNotebooks combines QC + clustering + annotation + GO enrichment + ambient-RNA correction into one long module; we split them across four shorter tutorials with paired Think about it prompts. Their dataset is GSE145926 (Liao 2020 COVID-19 BAL fluid, 4 patients); ours is ifnb.


Module 05 — Multi-sample integration (html)
Tutorial 05 — Two-Sample Integration
Same dataset (ifnb) and same two methods (Seurat anchors + Harmony) as ours. They add a quantitative neighborhood-mixing metric we don’t yet compute — see Adopted ideas below.

title: scNotebooks ↔︎ Workshop Crosswalk
text:
Topics we don’t cover (yet)
Modules 06–13 of scNotebooks extend into territory our workshop currently leaves to outside reading. They’re a natural next step.



scNotebooks module
What it covers
Worth opening?




Module 06 — Pseudotime / trajectory (html)
Monocle3 trajectory inference, pseudotime ordering, dynamic gene expression
Yes — for any developmental / differentiation study


Module 07 — Cell–cell communication (html)
LIANA: ligand–receptor inference, multi-method consensus
Yes — increasingly common in disease / immune work


Module 08 — Multimodal CITE-seq (html)
RNA + ADT (antibody-derived tags) joint analysis on CBMC data
Yes — the standard way to add surface-protein resolution to scRNA-seq


Module 09 — TCR profiling (html)
T-cell receptor sequencing with V(D)J + transcriptome
Mainly for immunology / vaccine / autoimmunity work


Module 10 — Spatial transcriptomics (html)
10x Visium pipeline in Seurat; spatial deconvolution
Yes — quickly becoming a core technique


Module 11 — scATAC-seq with ArchR (html)
ArchR pipeline: peak calling, motif enrichment, TF regulators, trajectory
Pairs naturally with our Tutorial 09 — scATAC-seq with Signac. Same biology, different toolkit (ArchR vs Signac). Read both for breadth.


Module 12 — Alternative polyadenylation (html)
SCAPE-APA: detection of poly(A) site usage from scRNA-seq
Specialist; useful if you suspect APA-driven regulation


Module 13 — FAIR data sharing (html)
Lecture 13 — FAIR Principles & Data Sharing + Tutorial 13 — FAIR Metadata & Submission
We adapted Module 13 into a full lecture + a hands-on tutorial that builds a CELLxGENE-conformant metadata sheet, converts the workshop’s ifnb_annotated_final.rds to AnnData, and generates BioSample/SRA/GEO upload TSVs.

title: scNotebooks ↔︎ Workshop Crosswalk
text:
Adopted ideas
A few things we picked up from scNotebooks while building our ifnb-based laptop sequence:

Same dataset for integration teaching. scNotebooks Module 05 uses ifnb exactly as we do in Tutorial 05. Independent convergence on the same choice is a good signal that it’s the right one for laptop-scale integration.
Per-sample HVGs before integration. Both curricula split the object by sample and run NormalizeData + FindVariableFeatures per sample before combining — see Tutorial 05 Step 1.
SoupX ambient-RNA correction. scNotebooks Module 04 walks SoupX in detail; we picked it up as Step 5 of Tutorial 01 (illustrative since ifnb’s filtered-only cache can’t run it directly, but the worked recipe is there).
scDblFinder doublet detection. Added as Step 6 of Tutorial 01, run per sample, with the scDblFinder.class == "singlet" filter folded into the QC subset in Step 7.
miloR differential abundance. Added as new Tutorial 08 — the compositional-shift complement to pseudobulk DE, on the same ifnb STIM-vs-CTRL contrast.
clusterProfiler functional analysis. Added as new Tutorial 07 — GO over-representation, GSEA, Reactome, and compareCluster cross-cell-type comparison on the pseudobulk DE table from Tutorial 06.
Spatial transcriptomics. Added as new Tutorial 11 — Visium QC, clustering, spatially variable features, and two-section integration on stxBrain (mouse brain anterior + posterior). Different platform (Seurat-Visium vs scNotebooks Module 10’s semla approach), same conceptual workflow.
Quantitative integration metrics. scNotebooks computes a per-cluster batch-mixing metric and a neighborhood-mixing score. Our Tutorial 05 uses a per-cell-type STIM-vs-CTRL ISG score gap as the over-correction diagnostic (a different but complementary check). Future revision could add a neighborhood-mixing entropy / LISI metric to make the side-by-side method comparison more numerical.

text:
How to use scNotebooks alongside the workshop

Browse: the scNotebooks website renders every module in three languages with copy-ready code cells.
Run on Colab: open any .ipynb directly in Google Colab — no local install. Their Colab tutorial walks through the upload step.
Run locally: their Docker image bundles everything.
Read PDFs of pre-run output: all modules ship as executed PDFs you can flip through without running anything.

title: Full Talapas RNA-seq Run — From Raw FASTQs
text:
Important



This is optional, self-paced material — beyond the three-day workshop. The in-class HPC track (Talapas 03 — Analysis Pipeline) runs the same ifnb dataset as the laptop tutorials and needs no raw reads. This page is for when you have your own raw 10x FASTQs (or want to reproduce a public dataset such as the 20k NSCLC DTC sample) and need the entire pipeline — from sequencer output all the way to differential abundance — on UO’s Talapas cluster.
This is a start-to-end roadmap: raw FASTQs → a counts matrix with Cell Ranger → the full analysis pipeline (the same numbered scripts as the in-class Talapas track), plus the bonus tracks. It is a first-pass guide that we’ll keep refining; everything it references already exists in the workshop materials.

title: Full Talapas RNA-seq Run — From Raw FASTQs
text:
Stage 0 — SLURM basics
If you’ve never submitted a cluster job, start with Talapas 01 — SLURM Basics: logging in, module load, interactive sessions, and sbatch. Appendix H — High-Performance Computing with Talapas is the deeper reference.

title: Full Talapas RNA-seq Run — From Raw FASTQs
section: Stage 1 — Raw FASTQs → counts matrix (Cell Ranger)
text:
Stage 1 — Raw FASTQs → counts matrix (Cell Ranger)
Talapas 02 — Raw Data Download + Cell Ranger count walks the whole BCL → FASTQ → counts path on SLURM:

how a 10x run goes from BCL → FASTQ (cellranger mkfastq) and FASTQ → counts (cellranger count)
installing Cell Ranger and the human reference on Talapas
a batch SLURM script — cellranger_count.sbatch — and scaling to many samples with a SLURM array job
inspecting the outputs: the filtered_feature_bc_matrix/ directory that Read10X() consumes

The end product of this stage is a filtered_feature_bc_matrix/ (barcodes / features / matrix) — exactly what the downstream pipeline reads.

title: Full Talapas RNA-seq Run — From Raw FASTQs
section: Stage 2 — Counts matrix → full analysis pipeline
text:
Stage 2 — Counts matrix → full analysis pipeline
From here the analysis is identical to the in-class Talapas track — the only change is the data source in step 01. The in-class scripts load ifnb from Bioconductor; to run on your own Cell Ranger output, swap the loader in 01_qc_preprocessing.R for Read10X():
# Replace the muscData loader in 01_qc_preprocessing.R with your matrix:
DATA_DIR <- Sys.getenv("DATA_DIR", "../data/filtered_feature_bc_matrix/")
counts   <- Read10X(data.dir = DATA_DIR)
if (is.list(counts)) counts <- counts[["Gene Expression"]]
seu <- CreateSeuratObject(counts, project = "myproject",
                          min.cells = 3, min.features = 200)
# ...then continue with the same QC / normalize / HVG / scale steps.
Everything downstream — 02–08 — runs unchanged, reading and writing .rds/.csv objects in ../objects/. See Talapas 03 — Analysis Pipeline for the script-by-script table, the run_rscript.sbatch wrapper, and submission commands.






Note



A note on study design. Real differential expression and abundance need genuine biological replicates and a real condition variable. A single dissociated-tumor run (e.g. one 20k NSCLC sample) has neither, so DE/DA on it only exercises the machinery. The in-class ifnb pipeline uses a real CTRL-vs-STIM design across 8 donors precisely so the results are meaningful — keep that in mind when adapting the scripts to your own data.

title: Full Talapas RNA-seq Run — From Raw FASTQs
text:
Stage 3 — Bonus tracks
The standalone scripts 09–13 (scATAC-seq, WGCNA, spatial, trajectory & cell–cell communication, FAIR metadata) parallel the bonus laptop tutorials and are documented in the same Talapas 03 — Analysis Pipeline page. Scripts 09–11 use their own datasets; 12–13 run on the annotated object the core pipeline produces.
For raw scATAC-seq reads specifically (the cellranger-atac count analogue of Stage 1), see scATAC-seq from raw FASTQs in Additional Resources.

title: Glossary
text: A working glossary of terms used throughout this workshop. Definitions are adapted from the Single-cell best practices glossary (Heumos et al.) and expanded where useful for this workshop.

title: Glossary
text:
A

Adapter sequences

Short, synthetic DNA or RNA sequences that are ligated to the ends of DNA or RNA fragments during library preparation for sequencing. Adapters are essential for binding fragments to the flowcell and enabling amplification and sequencing. If adapters are not trimmed after sequencing, they can appear in the reads and interfere with alignment and downstream analyses.

Algorithm

A pre-defined set of instructions to solve a problem.

Ambient RNA

Cell-free mRNA floating in the cell suspension that gets captured alongside a cell’s own transcripts, contaminating its expression profile. Tools such as SoupX or DecontX estimate and subtract it.

Amplification bias

A distortion that occurs during DNA or RNA amplification (e.g., PCR), where certain sequences are copied more efficiently than others. Amplification bias can lead to uneven or inaccurate representation of the original genetic material, affecting results in experiments like sequencing or gene expression analysis.

AnnData

A Python package for handling annotated data matrices, commonly used in single-cell and other omics analyses. AnnData stores data as a matrix where rows (observations) and columns (features) can have associated metadata and supports slicing, subsetting, and saving to disk in formats like H5AD and Zarr.

Anchors

Pairs of mutually corresponding cells identified across datasets during integration (Seurat CCA/RPCA). Anchors define the correspondences used to compute correction vectors that align batches before joint clustering.

Annotation

Adding labels to raw data to provide context and make it interpretable. Gene annotation labels genes with information like function, location, and associated proteins. Cell annotation classifies cells based on type, state, or function. Biological data can be annotated in many additional ways (e.g., based on batch, disease, sex).

Azimuth

A Seurat-based pipeline that annotates query cells by mapping them onto a curated, well-annotated reference (anchor-based label transfer), returning cell-type labels at several resolutions plus per-cell mapping and prediction scores.

title: Glossary
text:
B

BAM

Binary, compressed versions of SAM (Sequence Alignment/Map) files that store sequencing read alignments to a reference genome. BAM files contain the same information as SAM files — read sequences, quality scores, and alignment positions — but in a space-efficient format that enables faster processing and reduced storage requirements.

Barcode

Short DNA barcode fragments (“tags”) used to identify reads originating from the same cell. Reads are grouped by their barcode during raw data processing.

Batch effect

Technical confounding factors in an experiment that cause dataset distribution shifts. Batch effects usually lead to inaccurate conclusions if the causes are correlated with outcomes of interest and should be accounted for (usually removed).

Benchmark

An (independent) comparison of the performance of several tools with respect to pre-defined metrics.

Bulk RNA sequencing

In contrast to single-cell sequencing, bulk sequencing measures the average expression values across many cells. Resolution is lost, but bulk sequencing is usually cheaper, less laborious, and faster to analyze.

title: Glossary
text:
C

Canonical correlation analysis (CCA)

A dimensionality-reduction method that finds shared sources of variation between two datasets. In Seurat it is one way to identify integration anchors across batches.

Cell

The fundamental unit of life, consisting of cytoplasm enclosed within a membrane, containing biomolecules such as proteins and nucleic acids. Cells acquire specific functions, transition into different types, divide, and communicate to sustain an organism.

Cell Ranger

10x Genomics’ pipeline that turns raw sequencing reads (FASTQ) into a cell-by-gene count matrix, performing alignment, barcode/UMI correction, and cell calling.

Cell state

Cells can be annotated according to cell type or other states defined by the cell cycle, perturbational state, or other features.

Cell type

Cells that share common morphological or phenotypic features.

Cell type annotation

The process of labeling groups of clusters of cells by cell type. Commonly done based on cell type-specific markers, automatically with classifiers, or by mapping against a reference.

celldex

A Bioconductor package providing curated reference expression datasets (e.g., HumanPrimaryCellAtlasData, BlueprintEncodeData) used by SingleR for reference-based annotation.

Chromatin

The complex of DNA and proteins that efficiently packages DNA inside the nucleus and is involved in regulating gene expression.

Cluster

A group of a population or data points that share similarities. In single-cell, clusters usually share a common function or marker gene expression that is used for annotation (see cell type annotation).

clusterProfiler

An R/Bioconductor package for functional enrichment analysis — GO/KEGG over-representation and GSEA — used to interpret differentially expressed gene lists.

Codon

A sequence of three nucleotides corresponding to a specific amino acid or a start/stop signal in protein synthesis. Codons are the basic units of the genetic code.

Complementary DNA (cDNA)

DNA synthesized from an RNA template by the enzyme reverse transcriptase. cDNA is commonly used in RNA-seq library preparation because it is more stable than RNA and allows captured transcripts to be amplified and sequenced.

Conserved markers

Genes that mark a cluster consistently across conditions. FindConservedMarkers tests each condition separately and combines the p-values, so the marker is not an artifact of a treatment effect.

CpG

A DNA sequence in which a cytosine (C) is followed by a guanine (G) along the 5’→3’ direction, linked by a phosphodiester bond. CpG sites are often found in clusters called CpG islands near gene promoters. Unmethylated CpG sites are associated with gene activation, while methylated CpG sites can lead to gene inhibition.

title: Glossary
text:
D

Demultiplexing

The process of determining which sequencing reads belong to which cell using barcodes.

DESeq2

An R/Bioconductor package for differential expression of count data using a negative-binomial model with dispersion shrinkage; the standard tool for bulk and pseudobulk DE.

Differential abundance

Testing whether the proportion of a cell type or neighbourhood shifts between conditions (as opposed to expression changes within a cell type). Tools include miloR.

Directed graph

A graph consisting of nodes (vertices) connected by edges (arcs), where each edge has a direction indicating a one-way relationship between nodes.

Dispersion

In a negative-binomial model, the parameter capturing how much a gene’s variance exceeds its mean (overdispersion). DESeq2 estimates per-gene dispersions and shrinks them toward a fitted trend for stable testing.

DNA

Deoxyribonucleic acid. The organic chemical storing hereditary information and instructions for protein synthesis. DNA is transcribed into RNA.

Doublets

Reads obtained from droplet-based assays may be mistakenly associated with a single cell when the RNA expression actually originates from two or more cells (a doublet).

Downstream analysis

A phase of data analysis that follows the initial processing of raw data. In scRNA-seq, downstream analysis includes normalization, integration, filtering, cell type identification, trajectory inference, and studying expression dynamics.

Driver genes

Genes that actively control or “steer” a cell’s transition from one state to another during a biological process. Unlike marker genes, which merely identify a cell type, driver genes are functionally responsible for the fate decision at a bifurcation point.

Dropout

A gene with low expression that is observed in one cell but not in other cells of the same cell type. Dropouts commonly result from low mRNA amounts and the general stochasticity of mRNA expression. Dropouts are one reason scRNA-seq data is sparse.

Drop-seq

A protocol for scRNA-seq that separates cells into nano-liter sized aqueous droplets, enabling large-scale profiling.

title: Glossary
text:
E

Edit distance

Also called Levenshtein distance. The minimum number of operations (substitution, insertion, deletion) required to transform one string into another.

Elbow plot

A plot of the variance explained (or standard deviation) by each principal component, used to choose how many PCs to keep — the “elbow” marks where additional PCs add little signal.

Embedding

A way to represent complex objects (e.g., words, proteins, or genes) as numerical vectors so that computers can analyze them more easily.

Enrichment analysis

Methods that ask whether a gene set (e.g., a GO term or pathway) is over-represented among genes of interest. Over-representation tests use a fixed gene list; GSEA uses a ranked list.

title: Glossary
text:
F

FAIR

A set of data-stewardship principles — Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable — for making research data and metadata usable by both people and machines.

False discovery rate (FDR)

The expected proportion of false positives among the features called significant. p-values are adjusted (e.g., Benjamini–Hochberg) to control the FDR when testing many genes at once.

FASTQ

Sequencing reads saved in the FASTQ format. A FASTQ file stores DNA/RNA sequences and corresponding quality scores in a four-line format: identifier, sequence, optional description, and quality scores encoded in ASCII characters. FASTQ files are mapped against a reference genome to obtain gene counts for cells.

FindMarkers / FindAllMarkers

Seurat functions that identify genes differentially expressed in a cluster relative to the others (default: Wilcoxon rank-sum test). Useful for annotation, but not a replacement for replicate-level DE (see pseudobulk).

Flowcell

A consumable device used in sequencing platforms on which DNA or RNA fragments are sequenced. It has a glass or polymer surface with lanes or channels coated with oligonucleotides that capture and anchor fragments. During sequencing, fragments are amplified into clusters and their sequences are determined by fluorescent signal detection.

title: Glossary
text:
G

GEM (Gel Bead-in-Emulsion)

In droplet platforms (e.g., 10x Genomics), a single droplet containing one barcoded gel bead and ideally one cell, within which all of that cell’s transcripts are tagged with the same cell barcode.

Gene expression matrix

A cell (barcode) by gene (scverse ecosystem convention) — or gene by cell (barcode) — matrix storing counts as the cell values.

Gene Ontology (GO)

A structured, hierarchical vocabulary describing gene products by biological process, molecular function, and cellular component; the basis for GO enrichment analysis.

GSEA (Gene Set Enrichment Analysis)

A method that tests whether members of a gene set are concentrated at the top or bottom of a ranked gene list (e.g., ranked by fold change), without imposing a hard significance cutoff.

title: Glossary
text:
H

Hamming distance

A measure of the number of positions at which two strings of equal length differ. Commonly used in error detection and correction, including barcode correction in sequencing data.

Harmony

A fast integration method that corrects batch effects directly in PCA space by iteratively clustering and adjusting cell embeddings, producing a corrected reduction for downstream clustering and UMAP.

Highly variable genes (HVG)

The subset of genes with the most cell-to-cell variation beyond technical noise. Selecting HVGs (e.g., the top 2,000) focuses dimensionality reduction on the biologically informative features.

title: Glossary
text:
I

Imputation

The replacement of missing values with (usually artificial) values.

Indrop

A droplet-based protocol for scRNA-seq.

Integration

Aligning multiple samples or batches so shared cell types co-cluster while real biological differences are preserved. Methods include Harmony, Seurat CCA/RPCA anchors, and MNN.

title: Glossary
text:
K

k-nearest neighbors (kNN)

A graph in which each cell is connected to its k most similar cells (typically in PC space). The kNN — and the SNN derived from it — is the substrate for graph-based clustering and UMAP.

title: Glossary
text:
L

Leiden

A graph-based community-detection algorithm (Traag et al. 2019) that improves on Louvain by guaranteeing well-connected clusters. In Seurat it is algorithm = 4 in FindClusters().

Library

Also known as sequencing library. A pool of DNA fragments with attached sequencing adapters.

Locus

A specific position or region on a genome or transcriptome where a particular sequence or genetic feature is located. In sequencing, loci refer to the potential origins of a read or fragment (e.g., a gene, exon, or intergenic region).

Log-normalization

Seurat’s default normalization — divide each cell’s counts by its total, scale by a factor (10,000), and log-transform — making per-cell expression comparable.

Log2 fold change (LFC) shrinkage

Moderation of effect-size estimates so that low-information genes (low counts, high variance) are pulled toward zero, giving more reliable rankings (e.g., DESeq2’s apeglm).

Louvain

A modularity-optimizing graph-clustering algorithm; Seurat’s default in FindClusters() (algorithm = 1). Fast, but can occasionally produce poorly connected clusters — which Leiden fixes.

title: Glossary
text:
M

Marker gene

A gene whose expression is used as an indicator of a particular cell type, biological process, or cellular state. Marker genes are commonly used to identify or classify cells based on their function or identity.

Messenger RNA (mRNA)

A nucleotide sequence that has been transcribed from a gene and serves as a blueprint for a protein.

Metacell

An aggregate of a few transcriptionally similar cells, summed to reduce sparsity and noise. Used by hdWGCNA and similar methods before co-expression analysis.

miloR

An R package for differential-abundance testing on overlapping neighbourhoods of a kNN graph, reporting a per-neighbourhood log-fold change with SpatialFDR control.

MNN (mutual nearest neighbors)

An integration approach that identifies pairs of cells that are each other’s nearest neighbours across batches and uses them to compute batch-correction vectors.

Modalities

Different types of biological information measured at the single-cell level, including gene expression, chromatin accessibility, surface proteins, immune receptor sequences, and spatial organization. Combining modalities provides a more complete understanding of cell identity, function, and interactions.

Module eigengene

In WGCNA, the first principal component of a co-expression module’s expression matrix — a single per-sample summary value that is correlated with sample traits.

MuData

A Python package for multimodal annotated data matrices that builds on AnnData. The primary data structure in the scverse ecosystem for multimodal data.

Muon

A Python package for multi-modal single-cell analysis in Python by scverse.

title: Glossary
text:
N

Negative binomial distribution

A discrete probability distribution that models the number of successes in a sequence of independent, identically distributed Bernoulli trials before a specified number of failures. Widely used to model overdispersed RNA-seq counts.

Normalization

Adjusting raw counts to remove technical differences in sequencing depth and composition so that expression is comparable across cells (e.g., log-normalization or SCTransform).

title: Glossary
text:
P

PCR

Polymerase chain reaction. A method to amplify sequences to create billions of copies. PCR uses primers — short synthetic DNA fragments — to select the genome segments to be amplified and then multiple rounds of DNA synthesis.

Pipeline

Also called a workflow. A pre-specified selection of steps that are commonly executed in order.

Poisson distribution

A discrete probability distribution describing the probability of a specified number of events occurring in a fixed interval of time or space, with events occurring independently at a known constant mean rate.

Principal component analysis (PCA)

A statistical method used to simplify complex datasets by reducing the number of variables while preserving the main patterns in the data. PCA projects high-dimensional data onto orthogonal axes (principal components) ordered by the amount of variance they explain.

Promoter

A DNA sequence to which proteins bind (e.g., RNA polymerase and transcription factors) to initiate and control transcription.

Pseudobulk

Summing (or averaging) single-cell counts within each (sample/donor × cell type) group to create bulk-like profiles, so that DE can be tested with biological replicates as the unit of analysis — avoiding the pseudoreplication of per-cell tests.

Pseudotime

A latent, unobserved dimension reflecting cells’ progression through transitions. Pseudotime is usually related to real-time events but is not necessarily identical.

title: Glossary
text:
R

Reference-based annotation

Labelling cells by comparison to an annotated reference — either by correlation (SingleR) or by anchor mapping/classification (Azimuth) — rather than by manual marker inspection.

Resolution

The granularity parameter of graph-based clustering. Higher resolution yields more, smaller clusters; lower resolution yields fewer, larger ones.

RNA

Ribonucleic acid. A single-stranded nucleic acid present in all living cells that encodes and regulates gene expression. Unlike DNA, RNA can be highly dynamic: a messenger (mRNA) that carries genetic instructions, a structural or catalytic component (rRNA, snRNA), or a regulator of gene expression (miRNA, siRNA, lncRNA). RNA is central to transcription, translation, and cellular responses.

RNA velocity

A measure of the rate of change in gene expression, computed by comparing the ratio of unspliced (pre-mRNA) to spliced (mature) mRNA transcripts in single-cell RNA sequencing data. This ratio indicates whether genes are being actively transcribed (increasing expression) or degraded (decreasing expression), allowing researchers to predict the future state of cells.

title: Glossary
text:
S

SAM

Sequence Alignment/Map files. Tab-delimited text files that store sequencing alignment data, showing how reads map to a reference genome. Each line represents a single read alignment with the read sequence, base quality scores, mapping position, and mapping quality.

Scanpy

A Python package for single-cell analysis in Python by scverse.

SCTransform

A normalization method that models counts with a regularized negative-binomial regression, stabilizing variance and selecting HVGs in a single step — an alternative to NormalizeData + ScaleData.

Scverse

A consortium for fundamental single-cell tools in the life sciences that maintains computational analysis tools like scanpy, muon, and scvi-tools. See https://scverse.org/.

Sequencing

The process of deciphering the order of DNA nucleotides.

Shared nearest neighbor (SNN)

A graph derived from the kNN graph in which each edge is weighted by how many neighbours two cells share (Jaccard index). Seurat performs clustering on the SNN graph.

Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR)

A measure of the clarity of a signal relative to background noise. In sequencing, signal is the detectable information derived from the DNA or RNA molecules being sequenced, while noise includes random errors or unwanted signals. A high SNR indicates a strong, reliable signal and better data quality; a low SNR means noise may reduce accuracy.

SingleR

A reference-based annotation method that assigns each cell the label of the reference profile it correlates with most strongly (Spearman), with iterative fine-tuning and per-label confidence scores.

Slingshot

A trajectory-inference method that fits smooth lineage curves through clusters in a reduced-dimension space and assigns each cell a pseudotime along its lineage.

Soft-thresholding power (β)

In WGCNA, the exponent applied to gene–gene correlations to build a weighted network; chosen as the smallest β giving an approximately scale-free topology (R² ≳ 0.8).

SoupX

A tool that estimates and removes ambient RNA contamination (“the soup”) from droplet scRNA-seq counts, using the empty-droplet profile as the background estimate.

Sparse data

Data that mostly measures zeros and rarely other values (sparse data vs. missing data). Common in gene expression data, where many genes are not expressed in most cells.

Sparse matrix

A storage format for sparse data. Instead of keeping all zeros, a sparse matrix saves only the non-zero values and their positions, saving space and making calculations faster.

SpatialFDR

A multiple-testing correction used by miloR that accounts for the overlap between neighbourhoods on the graph — analogous to the FDR but weighted by neighbourhood connectivity.

Spike-in RNA

RNA transcripts of known sequence and quantity, used to calibrate measurements in RNA hybridization steps for RNA-seq.

Splice junctions

Locations where introns are removed and exons joined together in a mature RNA transcript during RNA splicing. Splice junctions occur at specific nucleotide sequences and are critical for the proper assembly of functional mRNA.

title: Glossary
text:
T

t-SNE

t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding — a non-linear method for visualizing high-dimensional data in 2D that emphasizes local structure. Largely superseded by UMAP for scRNA-seq.

Topological overlap matrix (TOM)

In WGCNA, a similarity measure between genes that also accounts for shared network neighbours; clustering on 1 − TOM groups genes into co-expression modules.

Trajectory inference

Also known as pseudotemporal ordering. The computational recovery of dynamic processes by ordering cells by similarity or other measures.

title: Glossary
text:
U

UMAP

Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection — a non-linear dimensionality-reduction method for 2D visualization that preserves local (and some global) structure; the standard scRNA-seq embedding plot.

Unique Molecular Identifier (UMI)

A special type of molecular barcode that uniquely tags each molecule in a sample library. UMIs enable the estimation of PCR duplication rates (see amplification bias), which supports error correction and increases accuracy.

Untranslated Region (UTR)

A segment of an mRNA transcript that is transcribed but not translated into protein. UTRs are located at both ends of the coding sequence.

title: Glossary
text:
V

Variance-stabilizing transformation (VST)

A transformation (e.g., DESeq2::vst) that makes a count variable’s variance roughly independent of its mean, useful before PCA, clustering, or WGCNA on bulk/pseudobulk data.

title: Glossary
text:
W

WGCNA

Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis — builds a weighted co-expression network, detects modules of co-regulated genes, summarizes each module as an eigengene, and correlates modules with sample traits.

Wilcoxon rank-sum test

A non-parametric test that compares two groups by rank; Seurat’s default marker test in FindMarkers / FindAllMarkers.



Definitions adapted, with modifications, from the Single-cell best practices glossary (Heumos et al.), licensed under the terms of that project.

title: Chapter 12 — Trajectory Inference & Cell–Cell Communication
text:
Note



Where this chapter sits. Companion to Lecture 12 and Tutorial 12. Prerequisites: an annotated, integrated object (Chapter 4, Chapter 5). A bonus chapter — these analyses are optional extensions of the core workflow.

title: Chapter 12 — Trajectory Inference & Cell–Cell Communication
text:
12.1 Two questions clustering cannot answer
The core workflow ends with discrete clusters carrying cell-type labels. Two common follow-up questions do not fit that discrete frame:

How do cells move between states? Differentiation, activation, and the cell cycle are continuous processes. Cutting them into clusters throws away the ordering. Trajectory inference models cells as points along one or more paths and assigns each a pseudotime — a position along the path, not a wall-clock time.
Which cell types signal to which? Tissues are coordinated by ligand–receptor signaling between cell types. Cell–cell communication inference predicts that wiring from expression.

Both build directly on the annotated, integrated object; neither replaces the clustering that produced it.

title: Chapter 12 — Trajectory Inference & Cell–Cell Communication
text:
12.2 Pseudotime and trajectory inference
A trajectory method (i) embeds cells in a reduced space, (ii) fits a graph, tree, or smooth curve through them, (iii) picks a root, and (iv) measures distance along that structure as pseudotime. Genes whose expression varies smoothly along pseudotime are the candidate drivers of the process.
Widely used tools:

Slingshot — fits smooth principal curves through the cluster structure; robust, needs a start cluster.
Monocle3 — learns a principal graph and supports branch points; learn_graph() then order_cells().
PAGA (scanpy) — builds an abstracted graph of cluster connectivity; the best first question is often “is there even a continuum?”, which PAGA answers well.
Diffusion pseudotime — random-walk distance from a root cell.

The single most important user choice is the root: pseudotime has no inherent direction, so the biologist must declare which end is the start (usually from a known progenitor marker). A wrong root reverses the entire narrative.
The deepest pitfall is more basic: the algorithm will return a trajectory even when none exists. Benchmarks (Saelens et al. 2019) show method choice matters enormously and that discrete data forced through trajectory tools produce confident nonsense. Decide a priori whether a continuum is biologically plausible.

title: Chapter 12 — Trajectory Inference & Cell–Cell Communication
text:
12.3 RNA velocity — adding direction
Pseudotime supplies an axis but not a direction. RNA velocity recovers the arrow by splitting reads into unspliced (intron-containing, newly transcribed) and spliced (mature) counts per gene. A high unspliced/spliced ratio means a gene is being induced, so the cell is heading toward a state with more of that transcript; the per-gene signals combine into a per-cell velocity vector that can be projected onto the embedding.
The original steady-state model is La Manno et al. 2018 (velocyto); the dynamical model in scVelo (Bergen et al. 2020) is the current default. Velocity needs a spliced/unspliced count matrix produced by velocyto or kallisto | bustools — not the standard filtered matrix — and assumes near-steady-state kinetics, so it is unreliable for shallow capture or fast processes.
CytoTRACE (Gulati et al. 2020) offers an assumption-light cross-check: less-differentiated cells tend to express more genes, so the breadth of detected genes is a proxy for differentiation potential. When Slingshot, RNA velocity, and CytoTRACE agree on the ordering and root, the trajectory is credible; when they disagree, that disagreement is the result to report.

title: Chapter 12 — Trajectory Inference & Cell–Cell Communication
text:
12.4 Cell–cell communication
scRNA-seq cannot observe receptor binding, but it can ask whether a ligand is expressed in one cell type and its receptor in another. Combined with curated ligand–receptor databases, per-cluster expression yields a predicted signaling network. Tools differ in emphasis:

CellPhoneDB (Python) — permutation test for significance; models multi-subunit complexes.
CellChat (R) — aggregates pairs into signaling pathways; strong circle/chord visualizations.
NicheNet (R) — links a ligand to the downstream target genes it should induce in the receiver.
LIANA (R/Python) — runs many methods/databases and reports a consensus.

The universal caveat: co-expression is not interaction. These tools report that a ligand and receptor are expressed in the right places, not that signaling happens. They ignore spatial adjacency (pair with spatial data, Chapter 11), secretion and diffusion, and the gap between mRNA and active protein; the databases are curated for human and mouse and are sparse elsewhere. Treat the network as a hypothesis generator and validate top hits (spatial co-localization, perturbation) before claiming a circuit.

title: Chapter 12 — Trajectory Inference & Cell–Cell Communication
section: 12.5 A note on long reads and isoforms
text:
12.5 A note on long reads and isoforms
Standard 3′ short-read scRNA-seq counts genes, not isoforms — it cannot tell which splice variant a cell uses. Pairing single-cell barcoding with long-read sequencing (PacBio Iso-Seq, ONT; e.g. scISO-seq) recovers full-length, isoform-resolved transcripts per cell. This connects back to the 3′ UTR annotation problem (Chapter 0 / Lecture 0): long reads both improve the annotations that short-read quantification depends on and enable per-cell isoform analysis — particularly valuable in non-model systems.

title: Chapter 10 — WGCNA: Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis
text:
Note



Where this chapter sits. Companion to Lecture 10 and Tutorial 10. Prerequisites: Chapter 6 (count modeling, normalization).

title: Chapter 10 — WGCNA: Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis
text:
10.1 The big idea
Differential expression and functional analysis (Chapters 6–7) ask “which genes change between conditions?”. WGCNA — Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis — asks a different question: “which genes change together across samples?”.
Genes that consistently rise and fall together across samples are likely functionally related — they participate in the same pathway, are co-regulated by the same TF, or are responding to the same upstream signal. WGCNA finds groups of such co-expressed genes (called modules) and connects each module to phenotypes via correlation with sample traits.
This is a systems-level analytical lens, complementary to per-gene DE. A module of 200 genes co-expressed and correlated with disease severity is often more informative than a list of 200 individually-significant DE genes.

title: Chapter 10 — WGCNA: Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis
text:
10.2 The network construction
Three steps build the gene co-expression network:

10.2.1 Pairwise correlations
Compute the Pearson correlation of every pair of genes across samples. The result is a gene × gene similarity matrix.


10.2.2 Power transform — the “weighted” in WGCNA
Raise the absolute correlation to a power \(\beta\):
\[a_{ij} = |\mathrm{cor}(x_i, x_j)|^\beta\]
This is the adjacency. Why power-transform? Real biological networks tend to be scale-free — a small number of genes have high connectivity (hubs), and most genes have low connectivity. Without a power transform, every pair gets a similarity score and the network is uniformly dense, hiding hub structure. With a power \(\beta = 6\) to \(12\), weak correlations are suppressed and strong ones are amplified, producing a network whose degree distribution looks scale-free.
The right \(\beta\) is data-dependent. WGCNA’s pickSoftThreshold scans a range of \(\beta\) values and reports the scale-free fit (\(R^2\) of the linear fit between log degree and log frequency). Pick the smallest \(\beta\) at which \(R^2 > 0.8\). For typical bulk RNA-seq, that’s \(\beta = 6\)–\(12\).


10.2.3 Topological overlap
Convert the adjacency to topological overlap matrix (TOM):
\[\mathrm{TOM}_{ij} = \frac{\sum_k a_{ik} a_{kj} + a_{ij}}{\min(\sum_k a_{ik}, \sum_k a_{kj}) + 1 - a_{ij}}\]
Two genes are TOM-similar if they have many shared connections, not just a high pairwise correlation. This makes the network more robust to spurious correlations.
The dissimilarity is \(1 - \mathrm{TOM}\), which is what’s clustered in the next step.

title: Chapter 10 — WGCNA: Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis
section: 10.3 Module detection — hierarchical clustering with dynamic cutting
text:
10.3 Module detection — hierarchical clustering with dynamic cutting
Run hierarchical clustering on the TOM dissimilarity matrix. The result is a dendrogram. To call modules, cut the dendrogram dynamically — cutreeDynamic finds branches whose internal connectivity is high relative to their connection to the rest of the tree.
Typical parameters:

minModuleSize = 30 — modules smaller than 30 genes are merged into a “grey” module of un-grouped genes
deepSplit = 2 — moderate sensitivity; higher values give more, smaller modules

The output is a colored module assignment per gene: each module gets a color label (turquoise, blue, brown, …) and the un-grouped genes get grey.

title: Chapter 10 — WGCNA: Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis
text:
10.4 Module eigengenes — the per-module summary
Each module’s expression profile across samples is summarized by its module eigengene (ME) — the first principal component of the module’s expression. The ME is one number per sample per module, capturing the dominant co-variation.
In R:
MEs <- moduleEigengenes(expr, colors = moduleColors)$eigengenes
The result is a samples × modules matrix. Now you can correlate each module against any sample-level trait (treatment, disease severity, time point, etc.) — the module-trait correlation:
trait_cor   <- cor(MEs, traits)
trait_pval  <- corPvalueStudent(trait_cor, nSamples)
Plot as a heatmap with significance asterisks. This is the canonical WGCNA figure.

title: Chapter 10 — WGCNA: Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis
text:
10.5 Picking a soft-threshold power \(\beta\)
Practical workflow:

pickSoftThreshold(expr, powerVector = c(1:10, seq(12, 20, 2))) — runs the scan
Inspect the output: at each \(\beta\), what’s the scale-free fit \(R^2\)?
Pick the smallest \(\beta\) at which \(R^2 > 0.8\)
If \(R^2\) never reaches 0.8 across the scanned range, your data is too noisy or has technical structure that isn’t being modeled. Don’t force it; investigate

Typical bulk RNA-seq: \(\beta = 6\)–\(12\). Bigger studies (more samples) can use higher \(\beta\) without losing connectivity.

title: Chapter 10 — WGCNA: Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis
section: 10.6 WGCNA on single-cell data — why classic WGCNA struggles
text:
10.6 WGCNA on single-cell data — why classic WGCNA struggles
WGCNA was designed for bulk RNA-seq, where you have, say, 50 samples each with one expression vector. Modules emerge from inter-sample correlation.
Applied directly to scRNA-seq, classic WGCNA struggles because:

Sparsity: at the cell level, most pairs of (gene, cell) entries are zero. Correlation of two sparse vectors is unstable.
Scale: 50,000 cells × 20,000 genes = 1 × 10^9 entries. The TOM matrix is genes × genes = 4 × 10^8 entries. Memory becomes a problem.
Heterogeneity: scRNA-seq has many cell types, each with its own co-expression structure. Mixing them gives a mash that doesn’t represent any single biology.

Two practical strategies:


Pseudobulk first. Aggregate scRNA-seq counts to (sample × cell type) pseudobulk (Chapter 6) and run classic WGCNA on the per-cell-type matrices. Often works well for 8+ samples.
hdWGCNA — a single-cell-aware reimplementation that uses metacells (groups of ~10-20 cells aggregated by cluster) as the unit and adapts the network construction for sparsity. Modern, recommended for scRNA-seq specifically.


Lecture 10 and the associated tutorial use the bulk workflow on the GSE152418 COVID-19 PBMC bulk RNA-seq dataset, since classic WGCNA on bulk is the foundational technique. For sc-specific WGCNA, see hdWGCNA.

title: Chapter 10 — WGCNA: Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis
text:
10.7 Reading module-trait correlation heatmaps
A typical figure: rows = modules (turquoise, blue, brown, …), columns = traits (severity score, age, sex, time point, …), each cell colored by Pearson correlation, with \(-\log_{10}p\) as text annotation.
Reading rules:

A module with strong correlation to one trait + weak to others → that module is “the X-response module”
A module correlated with multiple traits → either a confounded module or a true general-stress signature
No modules correlated with anything → either no signal in the dataset, or your module detection settings need tuning

title: Chapter 10 — WGCNA: Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis
text:
10.8 Hub genes and module export
Each module has hub genes — those most-connected within the module:
intramodConn <- intramodularConnectivity(adjacency, moduleColors)
hubs <- intramodConn |> arrange(desc(kWithin)) |> head(10)
Hub genes are biologically interesting candidates: a module’s hub is often the TF or upstream regulator coordinating the rest. Cross-reference hub genes against TF databases for hypothesis generation.
For downstream functional analysis, export the module gene list and run Chapter 7’s ORA / GSEA pipeline on it. WGCNA modules are gene sets — they enrich for biology like any other gene set.

text:

title: Chapter 8 — Differential Abundance: Do Cell-Type Proportions Change?
text:
Note



Where this chapter sits. Companion to Lecture 08 and Tutorial 08. Prerequisites: Chapter 5 — Integration (you need an integrated reduction), Chapter 6 — DESeq2: Bulk Fundamentals + Pseudobulk DE (parallel statistical machinery).

title: Chapter 8 — Differential Abundance: Do Cell-Type Proportions Change?
text:
8.1 The complementary question
Differential expression (Chapters 5–6) asks: for cells of the same type, which genes change between conditions? Differential abundance asks: do cell-type proportions themselves change between conditions?
These are independent questions. A perturbation can change cell-type composition, gene expression within types, both, or neither. A complete condition-level analysis reports both.
For example, in a scRNA-seq study of a viral infection vs control, you might find:

DE positive, DA negative: every immune cell shifts toward an antiviral state, but proportions are unchanged
DA positive, DE negative: a memory T-cell population expands in infected samples, but expression within each cell type is unchanged
Both positive: both populations and their per-cell expression change

The two analyses tell different parts of the story. Reviewers increasingly expect both.

title: Chapter 8 — Differential Abundance: Do Cell-Type Proportions Change?
text:
8.2 Why cluster-level proportion tests fail
The naive approach: count cells per (cluster, sample), make a 2×2 table per cluster, run Fisher’s exact / chi-squared. This breaks for three reasons:


Hard cluster boundaries are arbitrary. A cell type that spans two clusters at one resolution and one cluster at another gives a different test result. Resolution-dependent inferences are bad.
Within-cluster heterogeneity is invisible. A “T cell” cluster containing both expanding-activated and shrinking-naive subpopulations will show no net change at the cluster level — but real DA at finer resolution.
Cells aren’t independent samples. Cluster-level Fisher tests treat every cell as a replicate; the right unit is the donor, just like in DE.


The first two are particularly insidious. Cluster boundaries on a smooth biology gradient are dotted lines, not real ones, and proportion tests on dotted lines are unstable.

title: Chapter 8 — Differential Abundance: Do Cell-Type Proportions Change?
section: 8.3 The miloR approach — neighborhoods, not clusters
text:
8.3 The miloR approach — neighborhoods, not clusters
miloR (Dann et al. 2022, Nat Biotechnol) replaces hard clusters with overlapping neighborhoods on the kNN graph. Each neighborhood is a representative cell plus its \(k\) nearest neighbors; ~1000 neighborhoods are sampled to cover the data.
The procedure:

Build the kNN graph on the integrated PC reduction (the same one used for clustering)
Sample ~1000 neighborhoods (makeNhoods with prop = 0.1, refined = TRUE)
Count cells per (sample × neighborhood)
Fit a negative-binomial GLM per neighborhood with the design (~ donor + condition)
Apply SpatialFDR correction across overlapping neighborhoods

The output is a per-neighborhood log-fold-change in abundance and an FDR-controlled p-value. Since neighborhoods overlap, the corrected significance accounts for the correlation between adjacent tests.

title: Chapter 8 — Differential Abundance: Do Cell-Type Proportions Change?
section: 8.4 Why neighborhoods recover what clusters miss
text:
8.4 Why neighborhoods recover what clusters miss
Imagine a continuous biological gradient — naive T cells transitioning to effector. Hard clustering will draw a single boundary somewhere along the gradient and label one side “naive” and the other “effector”. A cluster-level proportion test sees the two clusters and reports their relative proportions.
If the perturbation shifts the position of the gradient (more cells now near the effector end), neighborhoods near the effector end show up-DA and neighborhoods near the naive end show down-DA. The cluster-level test, depending on where the boundary fell, might report the change correctly, or might miss it entirely if the boundary happened to sit in a stable region.
For continuous biology, neighborhoods almost always recover more signal than clusters. For very discrete biology (B cells vs T cells), they give the same answer. So neighborhoods are at worst equivalent and often better.

title: Chapter 8 — Differential Abundance: Do Cell-Type Proportions Change?
section: 8.5 Neighborhood size — the only parameter you’ll tune
text:
8.5 Neighborhood size — the only parameter you’ll tune
The defaults (k = 30, d = 20, prop = 0.1) work well for most 10–50k-cell datasets. The diagnostic is plotNhoodSizeHist(milo): the distribution of cells per neighborhood.
Target: median size between 50 and 200. Below ~30 the test is underpowered; above ~500 you’re spatially smoothing too much and losing fine structure.
If your peak is too small, increase k (try 50 or 75) and re-run. If too large, decrease k.

title: Chapter 8 — Differential Abundance: Do Cell-Type Proportions Change?
text:
8.6 The design and replication requirements
Same design framework as DESeq2:

~ stim — two-condition contrast, no other covariates
~ donor + stim — paired design (preferred when donors are balanced across conditions)
~ batch + stim — block on batch effects
~ severity — continuous covariate

And the same replication requirements as pseudobulk DE: at minimum 4 vs 4 biological replicates for moderate effects. With 1 vs 1 you get NA p-values everywhere — no degrees of freedom.






Warning



Don’t pseudo-replicate by splitting cells into “fake donors”. The workshop’s Tutorial 08 does this for ifnb (because the SeuratData distribution lacks donor IDs) but flags it as a teaching shortcut. Synthetic-donor pseudo-replication makes the test anti-conservative — its p-values have no biological meaning. For real DA inference, you need real donor IDs.

title: Chapter 8 — Differential Abundance: Do Cell-Type Proportions Change?
text:
8.7 Reading the signature plots

8.7.1 The neighborhood graph
Each dot is a neighborhood, sized by cell count, colored by log-fold-change (red = enriched in condition; blue = depleted). Faint = SpatialFDR > 0.1.
Look for:

Bright clusters of dots — a region of cell-type space that consistently shifts
Mixed regions — neighborhoods near each other with opposite effects (a sign of within-cell-type heterogeneity)



8.7.2 The DA beeswarm
plotDAbeeswarm(da_results, group.by = "seurat_annotations") plots each neighborhood’s log-fold-change as a dot, grouped by the cell-type label of the neighborhood’s representative cell.
Reading rules:

A cell type with most points above zero → enriched in the perturbed condition
A cell type with most points below zero → depleted
A cell type with points scattered above AND below zero → within-cell-type heterogeneity (some sub-states up, others down)

The third pattern is the case where neighborhoods recover what cluster-level testing misses. It’s also the most biologically interesting pattern — flag and investigate.

title: Chapter 8 — Differential Abundance: Do Cell-Type Proportions Change?
text:
8.8 The integration prerequisite
miloR builds neighborhoods on whichever reduction you give it. Use the integrated reduction, not the unintegrated PCA. Reasons:

If batch effects dominate the unintegrated kNN graph, neighborhoods cluster by sample, and the test “detects” composition shifts that are really batch artifacts
The biology you care about (cell-type proportion shifts) is best resolved when batch is corrected for

In Seurat: buildGraph(milo, k = 30, d = 20, reduced.dim = "HARMONY") (or "PCA" if integration was done in PCA space).

title: Chapter 8 — Differential Abundance: Do Cell-Type Proportions Change?
text:
8.9 Annotating neighborhoods
After the test, each neighborhood has a log-FC and SpatialFDR but no semantic label. annotateNhoods(milo, da_results, coldata_col = "seurat_annotations") assigns each neighborhood the modal cell-type label of its members. Use this to:

Generate the beeswarm plot (§8.7.2)
Summarize: count significant neighborhoods per cell type
Cross-tabulate against your manual annotations (Chapter 3)

title: Chapter 8 — Differential Abundance: Do Cell-Type Proportions Change?
text:
8.10 Common errors








You see
What’s wrong
What to do




reducedDimNames(milo) doesn’t include HARMONY

title: Chapter 6 — DESeq2: Bulk Fundamentals + Pseudobulk DE
text:
Note



Where this chapter sits. Companion to Lecture 06 and Tutorial 06 — DESeq2: Bulk Primer + Pseudobulk DE. Prerequisites: Appendix D — Statistical Foundations, especially §§ 1–3 (NB / Poisson / over-dispersion), § 4 (mean-variance relationship), §§ 5–7 (testing), § 8 (why per-cell DE fails).

title: Chapter 6 — DESeq2: Bulk Fundamentals + Pseudobulk DE
section: 6.1 Why we learn DESeq2 on bulk first
text:
6.1 Why we learn DESeq2 on bulk first
Pseudobulk differential expression for scRNA-seq (Part B of this chapter) is exactly bulk DESeq2 applied to per-cell-type aggregated counts. So we learn the bulk model in isolation here, on the canonical bulk dataset (airway from Bioconductor — 8 samples of dexamethasone-treated airway smooth muscle cells), and then in Part B we apply it almost mechanically to the single-cell aggregation.
This is the most heavily used statistical model in functional genomics. Earning a working understanding of it is worth several lectures.

title: Chapter 6 — DESeq2: Bulk Fundamentals + Pseudobulk DE
text:
6.2 The negative-binomial GLM
DESeq2 fits, for each gene, a generalized linear model:
\[\log(\mu_{ij}) = X_j^\top \beta_i + \log(s_j)\]
where:

\(\mu_{ij}\) is the expected count of gene \(i\) in sample \(j\)
\(X_j\) is the design matrix row for sample \(j\) (encodes condition, batch, etc.)
\(\beta_i\) is the per-gene coefficient vector (what we want)
\(s_j\) is the size factor for sample \(j\) — depth normalization, fitted separately

The likelihood is negative binomial:
\[Y_{ij} \sim \mathrm{NB}(\mu_{ij}, \alpha_i)\]
with per-gene dispersion \(\alpha_i\) that controls how much variance exceeds the Poisson baseline. The variance is \(\mu_{ij}(1 + \alpha_i \mu_{ij})\).
The choice of NB rather than Poisson is non-negotiable for RNA-seq counts. Poisson assumes variance = mean; real RNA-seq has variance > mean (over-dispersion), and Poisson testing is anti-conservative — it produces falsely-significant p-values. The NB adds a per-gene parameter to absorb the extra variance; results are honest. See Appendix D § 1–2 for the underlying distributions.

title: Chapter 6 — DESeq2: Bulk Fundamentals + Pseudobulk DE
text:
6.3 Size factors — depth normalization
Different samples have different sequencing depth. Without correction, a sample with twice as many total reads has twice the count for every gene, regardless of biology. The DESeq2 size factor \(s_j\) corrects this:
\[s_j = \mathrm{median}_i\left( \frac{y_{ij}}{(\prod_k y_{ik})^{1/n}} \right)\]
This is the median of ratios estimator. It computes a per-gene “geometric mean across samples” baseline, then for each sample takes the median of (sample \(j\)’s count / baseline) across genes. The result is robust — a few highly-expressed genes can’t dominate.
DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(...) and the subsequent DESeq(dds) call do this automatically; you don’t typically interact with size factors directly. But knowing the formula clarifies why DESeq2 is robust to a few genes shifting wildly between samples.

title: Chapter 6 — DESeq2: Bulk Fundamentals + Pseudobulk DE
text:
6.4 Dispersion estimation and shrinkage
Every gene has its own dispersion \(\alpha_i\), but with only a few samples per group, per-gene estimates are extremely noisy. DESeq2 borrows strength across genes by shrinking dispersion estimates toward a fitted trend (mean expression vs dispersion).
The procedure:

Maximum-likelihood per-gene dispersion estimates
Fit a parametric trend: log-dispersion as a function of log-mean
Shrink each gene’s estimate toward the trend, weighted by its uncertainty

The result: high-confidence genes (high counts, many samples) keep their MLE estimates; low-confidence genes (low counts) are pulled to the trend. The dispersions(dds) slot holds the final shrunk values; plotDispEsts(dds) visualizes the trend.
This is a Bayesian-flavored procedure — the trend is the prior, the per-gene MLE is the likelihood, the shrunk value is the posterior. See Appendix D § 7 for the connection.

title: Chapter 6 — DESeq2: Bulk Fundamentals + Pseudobulk DE
text:
6.5 The design matrix and contrasts
The design = ~ ... argument specifies which sample-level covariates affect expression. The simplest case:
DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(countData = ..., colData = ..., design = ~ condition)
Here condition is a factor with levels untreated and treated. The model has two coefficients per gene: an intercept (log expected expression in untreated, the reference level) and a conditiontreated coefficient (log fold-change of treated vs untreated).
For paired designs:
design = ~ donor + condition
This adds donor as a covariate, soaking up donor-level variation. The condition coefficient now estimates the treatment effect within each donor — much more powerful when donors are paired.
For interactions:
design = ~ donor + group + condition + group:condition
This tests whether the effect of condition differs between groups.
Always run relevel() to set your reference level explicitly:
dds$condition <- relevel(dds$condition, ref = "untreated")
If you skip this, R’s alphabetical default may pick the wrong reference, flipping the sign of every fold-change in your output. Hard to debug after the fact.

title: Chapter 6 — DESeq2: Bulk Fundamentals + Pseudobulk DE
text:
6.6 The Wald test and p-values
DESeq2’s default per-coefficient test is the Wald test:
\[z = \frac{\hat\beta - 0}{\hat{SE}(\hat\beta)}\]
Under the null (\(\beta = 0\)), \(z\) is approximately standard normal. The two-sided p-value is \(2(1 - \Phi(|z|))\).
For testing whether any level of a multi-level factor matters, use the likelihood ratio test (LRT):
dds <- DESeq(dds, test = "LRT", reduced = ~ donor)
This compares the full model (~ donor + condition) to the reduced model (~ donor); the LRT statistic is \(-2 \log(L_{reduced}/L_{full})\) and is \(\chi^2\)-distributed. Useful when condition has 3+ levels.
For both tests, the output table from results(dds) has columns:



Column
Meaning




baseMean
mean of normalized counts


log2FoldChange
effect size, base-2 log scale


lfcSE
standard error of LFC


stat
Wald statistic (or LRT statistic)


pvalue
raw test p-value


padj
BH-adjusted (the FDR you should filter on)

title: Chapter 6 — DESeq2: Bulk Fundamentals + Pseudobulk DE
text:
6.7 LFC shrinkage — never skip
Genes with very low counts (baseMean < 5) have huge LFC standard errors. Their raw log2FoldChange values are noisy and dominated by sampling luck. Sort the unshrunk results by LFC and your “top hits” will be a list of garbage low-count genes.
The fix: shrinkage:
res_shrunk <- lfcShrink(dds, coef = "condition_treated_vs_untreated",
                        type = "apeglm")
apeglm (Zhu, Ibrahim & Love 2019) is the recommended estimator. It pulls noisy LFCs toward zero, weighted by their uncertainty. High-confidence genes barely change; low-count noisy genes shrink dramatically.
Always shrink before:

Volcano plots
Ranking by effect size
Any “top genes” list

The unshrunk LFC is fine for hypothesis testing (the p-value cares about the SE-scaled LFC, not the LFC itself), but for ranking and visualization, shrunk values are far more honest.
The shrinkage is a Bayesian procedure with apeglm’s prior — see Appendix D § 7 for the connection to the dispersion shrinkage in §6.4. It’s the same idea: borrow strength from all genes to stabilize each gene’s estimate.

title: Chapter 6 — DESeq2: Bulk Fundamentals + Pseudobulk DE
section: 6.8 The full bulk DESeq2 workflow, in one block
text:
6.8 The full bulk DESeq2 workflow, in one block
library(DESeq2); library(airway)
data(airway)

dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(
  countData = assay(airway),
  colData   = colData(airway),
  design    = ~ cell + dex
)

# Pre-filter low-count genes (speed only — does not affect FDR)
dds <- dds[rowSums(counts(dds)) >= 10, ]

# Reference level (so log2FC sign means what you think)
dds$dex <- relevel(dds$dex, ref = "untrt")

# Fit
dds <- DESeq(dds)

# Get results for the contrast of interest
res <- results(dds, contrast = c("dex", "trt", "untrt"))

# Shrink LFCs for ranking and visualization
res <- lfcShrink(dds, coef = "dex_trt_vs_untrt", res = res, type = "apeglm")

# Filter to significant genes
sig <- subset(res, padj < 0.05 & abs(log2FoldChange) > 1)
nrow(sig)
Tutorial 06 Part A walks through this exact recipe with the airway dataset.

title: Chapter 6 — DESeq2: Bulk Fundamentals + Pseudobulk DE
section: 6.9 Independent filtering — what padj = NA means
text:
6.9 Independent filtering — what padj = NA means
You’ll see some genes have padj = NA even when their pvalue is small. This is independent filtering: DESeq2 automatically excludes very-low-count genes from BH adjustment, on the grounds that they have insufficient power to ever be significant and including them dilutes the FDR for the rest.
The filter is selected adaptively to maximize the number of detected genes at the chosen alpha. It is not a bug; it is making FDR more powerful. If you need to re-include filtered genes for a custom analysis, set independentFiltering = FALSE in results().
Cook’s-distance filtering also produces NAs: extreme outlier samples in a small experiment can break the dispersion estimate for one gene, and DESeq2 NAs it. Inspect with assays(dds)[["cooks"]].

title: Chapter 6 — DESeq2: Bulk Fundamentals + Pseudobulk DE
text:
6.10 Common errors (bulk)

What’s wrong
What to do

relevel() your factor before DESeq()


apeglm errors with “name not found”

This is normal; if you really want all genes, independentFiltering = FALSE

title: Chapter 6 — DESeq2: Bulk Fundamentals + Pseudobulk DE
text:
6.11 The cardinal sin
The single most-violated rule in scRNA-seq:






Important



Cells from the same donor are not statistically independent. If your experimental unit is the donor, your statistical unit must be the donor too — not the cell.


Per-cell differential expression (Seurat::FindMarkers between conditions) treats every cell as an independent observation. With 5,000 cells per condition, the effective N becomes huge, and the variance estimates collapse to almost zero. The result is anti-conservative p-values — thousands of “significant” genes that wouldn’t replicate in a new cohort.
This is documented empirically: Squair et al. 2021 (Nat Commun) showed that per-cell DE methods report 5–20× more “significant” genes than honest pseudobulk methods on the same data, with no corresponding increase in real signal. Most of those extra hits are technical artifacts inflated by pseudo-replication.
Pseudobulk DE fixes this. The fix is conceptually simple: aggregate per-cell counts to one observation per (donor, condition, cell type), then run a standard bulk DESeq2 model (Part A) on the aggregated matrix. The unit of test is now the donor, not the cell, and inferences are honest.

title: Chapter 6 — DESeq2: Bulk Fundamentals + Pseudobulk DE
text:
6.12 The aggregation step
For each (donor × cell type) combination, sum the UMI counts across all cells. The result:

Rows: genes (same as the per-cell counts)
Columns: (donor × cell type) pseudobulk samples — typically dozens, not thousands
Values: integer total UMI counts

In Seurat:
pb <- AggregateExpression(seu,
                          assays    = "RNA",
                          slot      = "counts",
                          group.by  = c("donor", "stim", "celltype"),
                          return.seurat = FALSE)$RNA
The output has columns named like donor1_CTRL_CD14Mono. Build a parallel colData data frame describing each pseudobulk column’s metadata:
meta_pb <- data.frame(
  group_id = colnames(pb),
  donor    = sub("_.*", "", colnames(pb)),
  stim     = sub("_[^_]+$", "", sub("^[^_]+_", "", colnames(pb))),
  celltype = sub(".*_", "", colnames(pb))
)
(Or build it from the original seu@meta.data with distinct() — more robust than parsing column names if your sample/cell-type names contain underscores.)

title: Chapter 6 — DESeq2: Bulk Fundamentals + Pseudobulk DE
Chapter 6 — DESeq2: Bulk Fundamentals + Pseudobulk DE
Chapter 6 — DESeq2: Bulk Fundamentals + Pseudobulk DE
section: 6.15 Why per-cell-type, not a single joint test?
text:
6.15 Why per-cell-type, not a single joint test?
You could imagine running a single pseudobulk DESeq2 with design = ~ donor + celltype + stim + celltype:stim and reading off the celltype:stim interaction term. Why don’t we?
Three reasons:


Different cell types have different dispersion structures. Mean-variance trends differ between, say, CD4 T cells and CD14 monocytes. A single dispersion fit pools across them and over-shrinks some, under-shrinks others.
Different cell types have different tested gene sets. A gene expressed only in monocytes shouldn’t be tested at all in T cells; the per-cell-type approach lets you filter the universe correctly.
Interpretation. Per-cell-type DE answers “in CD14 monocytes, which genes change?”. The interaction-test answer is “which genes change more in CD14 monocytes than in the average cell type?”. Both are valid questions but the per-cell-type framing is what biologists usually want.


The cost of per-cell-type DE is multiple tests per gene (one per cell type). FDR correction within each cell type is appropriate; cross-cell-type meta-correction is rarely worth it.

title: Chapter 6 — DESeq2: Bulk Fundamentals + Pseudobulk DE
text:
6.16 What the output looks like
Each row of de_all is a (gene × cell type) per-cell-type DE result. Filter:
sig <- de_all |> filter(padj < 0.05, abs(log2FoldChange) > 1)
sig |> count(celltype)
This gives you the per-cell-type “significant gene count”. For a strong contrast like ifnb STIM vs CTRL, expect 50–500 significant genes per major cell type (mostly ISGs and downstream). For weaker contrasts, expect a handful.
The resulting per-cell-type DE table is the input to:

Chapter 7 — Functional Analysis: turn the gene list into biological themes
Chapter 8 — Differential Abundance: the parallel question — do cell-type proportions change?

title: Chapter 6 — DESeq2: Bulk Fundamentals + Pseudobulk DE
text:
6.17 Replication requirements
Pseudobulk’s honesty depends on having enough donors. Power scales with the number of independent biological replicates, not cells:



Design
Power for moderate effect (LFC=1)




1 vs 1 donor
0% (no degrees of freedom)


2 vs 2
~20%


4 vs 4
~55%


8 vs 8
~85%



If you have only 2 vs 2, you can still run pseudobulk — it’ll be honest — but you should expect few significant hits and report sample size openly. If you have only 1 vs 1, no DE method can give you valid p-values; report descriptive fold-changes only.

title: Chapter 6 — DESeq2: Bulk Fundamentals + Pseudobulk DE
text:
6.18 The ifnb synthetic-donor caveat
The workshop’s ifnb dataset, as distributed by SeuratData, has lost the per-cell donor IDs from the original Kang et al. 2017 paper. To run a meaningful pseudobulk demonstration, the tutorial creates synthetic pseudo-donors by random cell assignment — 4 pseudo-donors per condition.
This is a teaching shortcut. The synthetic donors are not biological replicates, so the resulting p-values are not biologically meaningful. The workflow is correct; the specific p-values are not. If you want real pseudobulk on the Kang et al. dataset, load it via scRNAseq::Kang18Combine() from Bioconductor — that distribution preserves donor metadata.
For your own data with real donor IDs, the workflow gives valid inferences without modification.
